Go ahead, >> Joel. >> You and I were both both undrafted free agents. And when you got that call from the Bills, seeing that you posted something on social putting somebody through a table, who is that? How long did it take to convince them to do that? >> That's my uh that's my best friend, Dom. He's uh he and I have been best friends since we were four and it took all of uh two seconds to convince him. [laughter] It was >> Undertaker style. >> I got the call and we were so excited and we were like, "What's the Bills Mafia known for?" And my uh my brother-in-law was like, "Oh, they throw people through tables. You got to baptize yourself." I was like, "Well, I'm not going to do that." I was like, "Dom, can you do it?" And he was like, "All right, man. Let's do it." So, it was it was a good time. My dad sacrificed one of his long long long tabled picnic tables. What's it look like when you guys all get together as a group and you go out? who's ordering what? What's the damage? Who picks up the bill? How do you guys navigate this? >> So, billwise, we'll usually do like a credit card roulette. Um, if it's >> if it's out if it's out of season, >> but if it is during season, we go uh oldest to youngest um during the week. Every Thursday, we go out for like a O line dinner and uh we'll pick like a different spot in Buffalo. He [clears throat] uh >> he he likes his food. Not that he's, you know, >> a large human being, but he is, you know, but he he he just loves tasting food and I'm I'm with him on that. And so it's it's a great time. I I would say that we all order our fair share, but he's uh he's the one who likes to get it down. [laughter] >> H credit card roulette. I've had some scary times with that as an under pennies. Saving pennies and I was called on it. Very tough times. [laughter] >> Oh man. And it's this is before the NIL era. So it's you know you don't have undrafted coming out with six [laughter] figures in the account already, brother. >> It's crazy. Alec, you recently started a foundation. We would love to hear more about that. Tell us a little bit about it. >> Yes, sir. My wife and I, we just started the Anderson House. And so, what our stigma is or what we're really about is kind of uh it's it says healing starts here. And my wife and I both have some uh mental health issues and we both have anxiety and you know, stress about stuff that sometimes doesn't matter. And so we really wanted to bring that to light and especially for the youth because we think in this day and age everybody's so caught up with you know social media and that fake lifestyle and we want people to really understand that you know all that doesn't matter and you have to be able to work on yourself before you can really go out into the world and see the beauty of it for what it really is. And so we started this foundation of wanting to help kids who um are having a little bit of mental health disorders or not feeling the best about themselves to come out and speak about it. Um let me say so you you can go there and talk to them. Great job, Alex. >> That's a great one. I'm I'm gonna get that one framed up in the in the bedroom.

title: How defensive tackle Tommy Togiai emerged as Texans' 'Mr. Consistent'
text: Hi guys, Aaron Wilson. Had an opportunity to catch up with Texans strongman defensive tackle Tommy Tugi. One of the real key chess pieces in the Texans top ranked defense. One of the strongest guys pound-for-pound on the team. They pretty much have to kick him out of the weight room. Bench presses 500 lb, squats 700 lb. He's only 6'2 and 296 lb, but he looks a lot bigger than that because of how strong he is. And you think about Tommy, he's more than brute strength and force at the line of scrimmage. He's good at eluding blocks. He's good at getting into the back field, making big plays. But make no mistake, he does a lot of the dirty work. He's a real glue guy that keeps blockers off of Pro Bowl middle linebacker Aziz Alshshire. And he makes his own plays, too. But a lot of what he does is clog up the middle. and he is a great two gap scheme guy that can shoot the gap or control the middle of the defense. A true anchor in the middle of the defense. And his nickname is not just Mr. Consistent, which De Mo Ryan gave him. And that's a real nod, a badge of respect and recognition for Tommy, a former Ohio State standout, a former Gatorade player of the year back in Idaho where he's from. So you think about Tommy, they started calling him touchdown Tommy after his touchdown last season, that scoop and score against the Colts, a game they needed to make sure that they were all set for the playoffs. And that was in the regular season finale. There was a botched fullback play they had planned for him. It was going to be Buckeye to Buckeye handoff and it was a golden opportunity. CJ's supposed to hand the football off to him. He's lined up at fullback and he never got the football. Straoud saw that was crowded line of scrimmage to have a smooth handoff, so he kept himself for the touchdown. He wasn't being selfish, but they got the touchdown. But then he still got the touchdown. Tommy did later. And it's one of the reasons why they did that one-year $3.3 million contract extension for Togei because of the way he played. But outstanding season for Tommy and you know he had the fumble return for the touchdown and he's definitely one of the guys that to me for his size has extremely impressive speed. He's also one of the highest graded guys on the team and around the NFL for interior defensive lineman. A 74.2 overall pro football focus defensive grade. 15th among 134 qualified interior defensive line in the NFL. Pro Football Focus pass rush grade 71.5 that's 25th and he had a run defense grade of 65.0 I know. So, 26 in the NFL, 25 total pressures. He's a good pass rusher, two sacks, 20 hurries, three quarterback hits, 47 solo tackles. And as I said, I had a chance to talk with Tommy, and I can report this as I have before, but just to reiterate, there is mutual interest between the Texans and Tommy for a potential contract extension. nothing has started, but it's something that I believe will happen. And I just know how they feel about Tommy and the kind of football player and the kind of person he is. And where I caught up with him was at a great event. I was at the YMCA with Tommy and he invited teammates Solomon Bird and Junior Tofuna, fellow defensive lineman to be there with him. and Tommy and his wife, they were all there to hand out food to senior citizens, those in need through an organization called Second Servings nonprofit, which is to help food insecure people. So, there was some great stuff from Trader Joe's there for some senior citizens, and they filled up their wagons with food. There were some other NFL alumni there, and it was a nice I get to uh the honor of carrying some of the crates of food myself out from the trucks uh and helping to set up. So, it was uh really great for me to talk with Tommy about his passion for giving and also about football. So, we have an extended conversation. We'll have a part one and we'll have a part two and we'll start with part one. Now, just a little background on Tommy. As you guys know, he played for some other teams before he really hit stride here and initially he was on the practice squad. So, drafted by the Cleveland Browns, fourth round in 2020 and then 2021 draft, pardon me, and then plays for the Jacksonville Jaguars after two seasons in Cleveland, then back to Cleveland, then briefly the Atlanta Falcons, and he joined the Texans in 2024. And ever since then, he's done nothing but thrive for the Texans. And like I said, a good athlete, 498 in the 40-yard dash. And I thought last season just especially when they needed him to step in with Tim Settle Jr. going down with that broken foot. Uh that's when he stepped up and he started six games for the Texans. But in just six games and he had limited action before that. 59 tackles total and six of those were for losses or rather it's five quarterback hits, one fumble recovery, four passes defense. And I think this is wrong. on. They got him down for one and a half sacks. I believe it's two whole sacks and of course all those solo tackles. So, a good job done by Tommy Tigi playing 15 games and starting six of them. And I think the best is yet to come for Tommy Tigi and know just appreciative of his time. And of course, he also started both playoff games and he had 13 tackles and a forced fumble against the Steelers and Patriots combined, including two tackles for losses and five solos. All right, guys, let's hear from Tommy right now. and we get into several topics including the potential for a contract, about his giving with the YMCA and about his workouts and his nicknames and being a part of a defensive line group headlined by Will Anderson Jr. and Denil Hunter and just uh feeling really good about all the confidence that they have in him and everything that goes along with that. All right, guys. Right now, Tommy Tai, >> right? As you said, the perspective of helping people and kind of where does that come from and uh you know, from your heart to want to give back and to help the community. >> I think just like being raised like in the Polynesian culture like you know, we're always about family and like helping those in need. So, I think like growing up with that uh cuz also like my family like we all I mean I think everyone always needs help. You know, there's no no uh reason for no one to like be able to not reach out for help. So being able to give back too is like very big for me and my family and to be able here be today and uh see the people coming through and that that we can help them in a in a certain way is a big big thing for me. >> What did you learn about second servings in the organization cuz it's it's a very in-depth thing where they have to get, you know, relationships with the grocery stores and then organizations like the YMCA and then having that outreach. >> Yeah. No, it's awesome to see to get to know their organization, Second Service, know they're doing a great thing what they got going on. Uh, you know, with the food trucks being driven out to the grocery stores, bringing them back and then unloading them for everybody to have a chance to come through and everything. So, I think it's just really awesome to see and see how the things operate behind the scenes, not just the product, like giving back to the people when they come through, but they're doing a lot of the things behind the scenes that maybe a lot of people don't want to do and all that. They put you and Solomon and the other guys, Junior, all to work today and it's like your second workout. I know that you were in the weight room probably this morning, but then uh you get another workout. >> Yeah, I know. I told the guys Yeah. cuz we had another workout. Yeah. This morning and I was just letting them know like if you guys I'm doing this event like just to help people in need and they're they're all in. Like I even I just asked them day before and they're like yeah we'll come help out. So just shout out to those guys to be able to be here with me helping out too today. What is the culture like in the defensive line room? I've heard there's a ton of nicknames and I can't remember them all. I know that Will is Terminator, Denil is Cyborg. >> Do you have a nickname? >> Uh yeah, they just called me shoot Mr. Reliable. >> Mr. Consistent. >> Yeah, that also. >> I think that's a good nickname to have. >> Yeah, I know. Definitely. You know, I'm grateful for like whatever nicknames I'm cool with. Tommy T. I was like a lot of guys TT. Yeah. >> What's it like in the room? The camaraderie. Obviously like you know you guys are like a family. >> No it is that I think we got a really close-knit group guys that you know want to achieve to the highest level and I think that's what drives everybody in that room that we want to be the best and I think you can see it like we push one another when we get together in practice and all that. So I think very uh very close-knit group and you know we all want to get we all have the same goal in mind. >> You think about last season and you have top ranked defense. What was it like? Pride to be a part of a defense that was first in both categories most of the year. Wound up finishing first in the one that they use the yards and second in points and obviously there was some substituting in the final regular season game which did uh allow the Broncos to one up with that one. But you have the number one the one that people care about which is yards. That's where the measuring stick comes from for having the top defense. You know, I'm just very grateful. Yeah. To have the opportunity to be, you know, a part of the Texans and especially this defense, man. It's just coming to work every day is like it's fun honestly to be part of this defense. So like I think yeah, like I said, not just the D line, but the whole defense like everyone has the mentality of like that swarm and go fly around, try to make plays. Everyone like every single snap, everyone's trying to make a play. Like I think everyone having that mentality on defense, it's something special. >> What do you attribute your You've been obviously you're a blue chip football player. You play at Ohio State and you get drafted, but then you move around to a couple of teams. It seems like you were trying to kind of find your way in the NFL. What was it about the Texans where everything clicked for you? >> I think honestly, yeah, like for me, just learning from previous years, like through my career, like always learning, taking away something, and then applying it to me like the next year. So I think then once I got to the Texans, I knew how to kind of highlight the stuff that I need to show and be able to produce what I needed to on the field. So just learning from those past experiences and always stay believing in myself. Think about individually um some of the things that you did last season like you said that when they call you Mr. Consistence because every practice, every game you're bringing the effort and you're making plays but you're doing it within the framework of the defense which is Dico Ryan's insist on. It's not hero ball where you make a tackle like it's because you're supposed to make the tackle or the play is uh there and you have to make the stop. >> What do you think about in terms of confidence and you fitting the scheme? What are some of the things that kind of coincided with you here? Yeah, I think like I said before like believing in myself at an all-time high like going out there believing I can make the plays that I can make and like you said like the Miko Leah he expects a lot from this defense which we should because we have so many guys that can go make the plays and can do the right things and most of the time we always say like offenses don't score on us like without us being like making a mistake ourselves. So it's like the offense didn't do anything. It's more the defense we did something wrong. That's the reason why maybe you see something happen or something like that. But yeah, I think for me, yeah, like to be able to produce uh the way I did last year is just was the technique learning from yeah, playing in the system, but also like just the belief in myself and knowing how hard I work like outside of the building and doing the things I need to do to prepare myself to be ready when game day comes. >> Everyone says it's a Super Bowl caliber defense, but football is a team sport. So, the biggest thing is like it doesn't matter so much if they say, "Well, the defense is this level." It's about the team. When you think about the opportunity for the team to take those next steps to try to get past the divisional round, it's been three years in a row and for the organization seven times in the divisional round. >> What is that like? Obviously, it hurts to to not there there's only going to be one happy team at the end of the year. This team trophy, but >> it, you know, I know you guys want to >> obviously push the football further and there's only one goal, which is to get to a Super Bowl and win a championship. How do you guys uh sort of emotionally compartmentalize it all and kind of put it all together? >> I think for the most part, yeah, like I remember Will early in OTAAS, he talked about like just doing more like everybody like just doing more. Uh if you think you're doing enough, you're not. So I think like having that mentality, if everyone can have that mentality, it's going to be really special this season. And who knows, maybe there'll be more things like that as you continue to grow within the organization because you've proven yourself now. And they've said that. So I I tend to take like a lot of things that go off of actions, not words. So when they, >> you know, when they do that, when they commit to someone, I say, "Okay, they're telling me with their actions, like with Will Anderson, yeah, >> that's someone we want to be a core piece of it." title: Tennessee Head Coach Heupel on Rookie Colton Hood | Giants Huddle | New York Giants
text: Welcome to another edition of the John Schmelk podcast, brought to you by Citizens, the official bank of the Giants. I am John Schmelk. Thank you so much for being with us, everybody. Our series continues in this offseason getting ready for the year. A little bit earlier in the offseason, we talked to some of the college coaches of Giants draft picks. Today, we're going to be joined by the head coach of the Giants second-round pick, Josh Heupel. But just a reminder, if you haven't checked out the episodes yet, uh the last, I don't know, dozen to 15 episodes of the John Schmelk podcast is our position series talking to players at different positions on the Giants um about those position groups. And before that, uh a lot of Giants assistant coaches talking about their journey and how they got here. And uh a little bit about how they're coaching up their position groups as well. So, make sure you go check those out. And without further ado, joining me from the Hackensack Meridian Health Podcast studio, Keep Getting Better, is the head coach of the Tennessee Volunteers, Josh Heupel. Coach, how are you today? >> Doing great. Great to be on with you guys here today. >> No, I I appreciate you joining us. Um so, let's talk about Cole Hood, the the Giants second-round pick. We've had a chance to be around him in the spring. And I want to start here with with him as just a guy. What an effervescent kid. Just very forward, type A personality. He has been an absolute pleasure to be around. >> Yeah, uh you know, came to us in in the late spring uh a year ago and uh dynamic personality. Guy that's infectious energy every single day. Cares about the guys around him. Uh you know, developed relationships with those guys, garnered their trust really quickly. And a guy that's going to, you know, go prove it on the field. Uh he's going to come to work every single day and go earn it. >> Now, you deal with this a lot. Transfers come in in their first year. How quickly did he fit in? How quickly did he assume a leadership role with the Jermaine McCoy injury? How did he quickly learn your system and kind of get in the mix having been a late arrival in June? >> Yeah, our guys came back uh late part of May. He actually got here a couple weeks early. Uh just wanted to get his feet on the ground and start to get an understanding of what we're doing defensively. Um you know, get adjusted to the weight room. Uh and uh you know, the as soon as the rest of our team came back, again, a guy that's extremely humble, but you can tell cares about his teammates, started developing relationships with them right away. And as the summer went on and he had his feet fully entrenched in what we were doing defensively, had great command of everything. And throughout the course of the year, just continued to grow in a leadership role. But it all started by him just going to work every single day, being consistent, being one of the first guys in the building, last one to leave, doing extra work. You know, he's a guy that, you know, played corner, but he was learning nickel at the same time. There were a lot of things that were on his plate and did a great job of, you know, learning and growing inside of our system and then, you know, developing a leadership role and obviously played extremely great football. >> Yeah, I I I want to get to the nickel stuff in a second. What attracted you to him? Why did you bring him in, target him in in the transfer portal? Why did you want him part of your program? >> Yeah, you see the physical attributes first, length, speed, ability to change direction, had great zone understanding, understanding relationships, bodies, route combinations and then certainly has all the physical traits to to do a great job in in man coverage as well. And you know, we had the injury to Jamar. He came in, learned it, earned it and took a job extremely quickly and you know, throughout the course of the season, he continued to get better. Not just every week, but every single day. He's hyper-focused when he gets his feet on the grass in in a practice situation or in the meeting room, completely dialed in and that was infectious and spread throughout our defensive unit as well. >> Now, I I know it's much more common now in college football and I'm sure once you talked to him, you know, his personality kind of, you know, made the decision easy. But when you see a kid that would be in his third school in three years, is it something that you still have to do a little bit more work into to figure out, all right, well, why hasn't this worked in the prior two stops, but it will work with us? >> Yeah, certainly. You know, you see the tape and then I didn't hit on it in your previous question, but they came to campus, him and his family came to campus. You know, they're interviewing us, but we're interviewing them at the same time and trying to figure out, you know, what was the why behind it. He had very pointed things that were reason of why he was transferring and you get a chance to to get around him and his family. They're they're tremendous people. You know, they want to live life the right way. They want to be a part of a team setting. He wants to be coached hard, but he wants an opportunity to grow and and be around like individuals. You know, they care about the people around them, they care about the organization and ultimately want to go win. >> He's a big family, too. Did he bring all seven siblings with him or was it just the parents? >> We didn't we didn't have all seven. We had a good contingency of them and they certainly showed out every week no matter whether we were at home or on the road. It's a it's a a really close-knit family. >> Was the intention to have him play nickel when when you first brought him in and and as someone seeing him play now, seeing him as an outside guy and how good he is out there, what was your thought process that, all right, well, we can maybe plug this guy in a nickel here if we need him. >> Yeah, there were some unknowns from us on the defensive side of the football with Jermaine's injury that he sustained in in January. You know, what was his timeline? Was he going to have an opportunity to get back or not? Some question marks at nickel. We saw him as somebody that absolutely could play on the edge and and play corner and and play that at a high level in in zone and man principles, but also had the skill set, the understanding once we got him here to campus and and talked ball with him. A guy that would fit in at that nickel position really seamlessly as well. >> Yeah, what was it about the physical traits that you mentioned a couple of these in your previous ads are that you thought, all right, we can slide him outside now and he can work as a perimeter corner in the SEC going up against basically the top wide receivers in the country? >> Yeah, has great length, has great speed, has really good change of direction for his length, has the ability to to play the deep ball, he doesn't panic in those situations. You know, he's got wide receiver type skill sets when the ball is up in the air. You know, he's willing to stick his face on people and and be physical as well. And you know, that's one of the areas that he grew throughout the course of the year. And you know, like I said, he got better every single week. His best football is still in front of him. And I think he's going to continue to grow with the Giants. >> You mentioned the no panic with the ball in the air. Is that something guys just have naturally? Is that something that you help develop with coaching? Because to me that really is is a key. You don't commit those defensive pass interference penalties down the field if you don't panic. Just talk about that aspect and kind of how he developed it or is that something that just kind of he had inside of him? >> Yeah, it's something that we're going to work, we're going to train. We want our guys to continue to get better at that. Putting our wide receivers and DBs in contested situations down the field where they're learning how to to play, play the man and play the ball. Being able to track and locate it. You know, how to defend it if you're only going up with one. How to go high point it with two. But I think for a lot of those guys, the more time that they've spent in those situations you know, as a young guy playing wide receiver where you know, they're getting a bunch of work at that. I think that becomes a part of them and it's ingrained in them and it transfers over to the defensive side of football as well. >> You mentioned he grew in terms of physicality around the line of scrimmage. Now it's to the point where he looks like he really enjoys that. And that's how he wants to play. When you see a corner, does that get you excited as a coach when he wants to be that physical player at the line of scrimmage? >> Yeah, absolutely. It gives you the the luxury and the freedom to to be multiple in in your defensive structures and calls. The ability to use him in some of the run game depending on the formation and the structure of your defense. You look at perimeter screens off of RPO. He's got the ability to destruct blocks. title: 49ers UPDATE: Ricky Pearsall turns heads...
text: To be honest, Deebo Samuel might fit best with the Chiefs who have a dink and dunk quarterback like Patrick Mahomes. For an aggressive downfield passer like Brock Purdy, Ricky Pearsall is a better receiver fit. But it's not an either or. 49ers might end up with both Pearsall and Deebo Samuel on a prove-it type deal, layering the depth of their wide receiver room. I want to talk about both of these guys, but the Pearsall workout video is a good place to start. Got to love the compression sleeve on that right knee. Doing what he can to prevent a recurrence of the PCL injury that hurt him last year. Ricky Pearsall, when he was fully healthy last year, over the course of the first four games, was a top-seven yards per route run receiver. I think it's really, really important to emphasize how good Ricky Pearsall has been when he's been healthy. And even if you factor in the injury for Ricky Pearsall, look at the yards per route run over the course of the entire season. He was playing hurt for most of it in 2025. Look how he ranks against his fellow 2024 wide receiver draftees. Behind only Malik Nabers last year. So, yes, ahead of Ladd McConkey, ahead of Marvin Harrison Jr. And it was 2.27 yards per route run over the first four weeks. As I said before, that PCL injury happened in week four against Jacksonville. By the way, the injury didn't happen on the hip-drop tackle at the start of that game. It happened when Pearsall slammed his knee onto the ground trying to make a catch near the sideline on a great throw from Brock Purdy. And I think it actually was a great catch from Ricky Pearsall. He showed me a picture of it. He had both feet in bounds and he secured the football, but the officials called it an incompletion. So, that was insult on top of injury because he did get hurt on the play. But, 2.27 yards per route run, that's very good. Anything over two is considered solid. Anything over three, that is elite. Brandon Aiyuk, for example, was awesome for the 49ers in that 2023 season. I think that we should take a second to acknowledge how good Brandon Aiyuk was in 2023. Just a quick little diversion here. He was number one in yards per catch, 18.1 yards per catch. Number two in yards per route run. I just showed you Pearsall 2.27 when he was healthy last year was good. Aiyuk was over 3 yards per route run in 2023. He had the highest first down rate in 12 years, 58.1% of Aiyuk's catches went for first downs in 2023. And he had the highest ever DVOA, defense adjusted value over average, the stat uh created by Aaron Schatz, formerly of Football Outsiders. It beat Jerry Rice's 1989 number. That's how good Aiyuk was in 2023. Uh I know a lot of 49ers fans don't like the guy anymore. I you know, you could understand why, but I think it's important to acknowledge just how awesome he was in 2023 in the efficiency department because it helps us explain why Kyle Shanahan rammed that contract across the finish line. Obviously, the 49ers very quickly regretted the deal, but because they were in a mode to try to run it back and Aiyuk was delivering those types of numbers, well, uh it it makes sense why they wanted to make sure that he was secured moving into the future. Back to Ricky Pearsall, though, cuz Ricky that is not an X wide receiver. The The X for the 49ers is Mike Evans. They've needed that position filled ever since they lost Brandon Aiyuk. So, Mike Evans has taken over the X for the 49ers. Can they get over 3 yards per out run for Mike Evans? Probably not. That's a lot to ask, but if they can get a solid 2 yards per out run, the 49ers actually feel that they are now stronger at the Z than they really have ever been. They used that first-round pick on Ricky Pearsall in 2024. And again, we we talk about if he can stay healthy, the 49ers have a guy who's been producing at the Z receiver position. Somebody who matches well with Brock Purdy. Purdy was at 9 yards average depth of target early in his career, 2023 and 2024, which is exceptionally high. Somebody who really pushes the ball downfield. You look at when they had Ricky Pearsall against the Seattle Seahawks healthy in week one, that very first long third down on the touchdown drive that ended with the toss from Purdy to Kittle. It was Brock Purdy layering a throw over 20 yards, middle of the field, seam shot to Ricky Pearsall. Pearsall's smoothness pairs very well with Brock Purdy's accuracy. Remember the game-winning drive and it with the Jake Moody touchdown? It was Ricky Pearsall on the double move. Brock Purdy found him with a perfect perfect pass. So, when they had Ricky healthy against the Seahawks, the 49ers beat Seattle, which was one of the all-time great defenses last year. And he was operating from that Z receiver position. When Ricky wasn't healthy, which was everything but week one against Seattle, well, obviously, the Seahawks defense smothered San Francisco. So, the Z position is one that I think is built for Ricky because the Z can come in motion. It's the flanker, right? The Z can get a little bit of a moving start. I don't want to say a running start, but a moving start. The X, that's perfect for Mike Evans. It was great for Brandon Aiyuk. It was that boundary receiver that was locked into a spot. We call him the split end. Also really important to block in that run game very well. 49ers now have the X, which should help spring Ricky Pearsall open coming out of motion at the Z. Then there's the F position and this is where they've invested a ton obviously through the draft and De'Shawn Shribling is somebody who could I think reprise the Jauan Jennings role for the 49ers. At F, which is the slot inside receiver position, the 49ers I think will love to have the adaptability that they have this year that they may not have had in the past because of injuries and because they didn't have the talent they do now. But they can either go small slot, which is a shiftier slot receiver like a Christian Kirk, who is also very fast and we'll talk about the utility of that in a little bit. Or they can go to big slot to increase blocking potential and also to create mismatches with size and that's De'Shawn Shribling who's what, 6'3 and can run at 4.36. So he can bring a lot more speed to the big slot than Jauan Jennings brought. Jacob Cowing, probably a small slot receiver, but he's got burner speed. Also a mix into that depth chart for the 49ers. Then comes the positional versatility for the 49ers in the wide receiver room. De'Shawn Shribling and Christian Kirk may both be based at the F, at the slot. Big slot, small slot, but De'Shawn can also play the X and maybe down the road he takes over that X receiver position after Mike Evans is done. Or if Mike Evans is hurt or if Mike Evans needs a breather, De'Shawn Shribling has the two things that you need to play X and that is size and speed. 4.36 speed, 6'3 size. We saw the picture here from Tennessee. This is our last video by the way from Nashville studio heading out to California today. But we saw from Deebo Samuel Stribling here in Tennessee picture taken next to George Kittle looked about to be George Kittle size. He might have been a little bit closer to the camera than George. So maybe a slight optical illusion. But we know that Deebo Samuel Stribling is a big guy who can flex to the X. And we know that Christian Kirk is a fast guy experienced receiver who can flex to the Z. Then you enter all these Deebo Samuel rumors. And I know that Kyle Juszczyk and George Kittle have both been talking about hosting Deebo Samuel in their respective guest houses. The quickest mistake and the most common mistake somebody can make when it comes to talking about the 49ers potentially bringing in Deebo Samuel is thinking that they're going to bring in a 2021 to Deebo Samuel at $10 million or more. That's not what it would be. In fact, if Deebo were being offered $10 million or more, he would have already signed right now. This is 30-year-old Deebo who if he joins the 49ers, it would be on a much smaller deal and it would be a layering of depth for the 49ers. It wouldn't be oh, let's bring Deebo Samuel in and automatically kick somebody else out. It would be it's July 20th in each of the past two seasons the 49ers receiver core has looked way different at roster cut down day than it did on July 20th. And it's looked way different in a in a bad way because there's been so much attrition. So the 49ers would be smart to layer as much economical depth as possible into that wide receiver room. title: Green Bay Packers ownership change 'could happen' - Mike Florio | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: One last topic and I want to properly lay the foundation before an army of cheese heads is lined up outside of my window. And I think if this ever happened, it wouldn't change anything for Green Bay Packers fans with one exception that I'll get to. I believe at some point in the past four weeks, five weeks, however long we've been doing this during the PFT live break, this is week number six, so we've been doing it for five. A question came up about the Packers and their structure and the public ownership. And I I can't remember if it was about buying up the stock. I mean, the reality is the Packers for decades have been a corporation and the shares are owned by individual fans who receive a certificate that is suitable for framing and putting in the man cave. And you can say we because you own a piece of the team. But when they do the stock sales, they have all sorts of disclaimers and limitations. You can't resell it. No one can go out there and buy up all the Green Bay Packers stock or at least enough of it to have a hostile takeover. That's not how it works. It's not like a normal corporation. You can't sell it for a profit. You're basically donating money and getting this piece of memorabilia. Yes, you own a piece of the team, but what do you ultimately own? Nothing tangible. Nothing that is going to pay anything to you. It's sentimental value, and it anchors the team in Green Bay. For as long as Green Bay Packers Incorporated exists, the Packers will always be in Green Bay. This has come up because President Ed policy, who took over last year, has publicly lamented the fact that the Packers ownership structure prevents them from doing the things that other teams can do to raise money. The Packers can't sell a little sliver here, a little slice there, a percentage point here for $500 million, whatever the valuation would be. They can't raise that money the way that other owners can. And now the private equity can come in and buy up to 10% of a team. That's cash that the Packers will never have access to. and it creates a potential competitive disadvantage. Now, is this part of a broader leverage play to get better terms from the local governments as they try to renovate the stadium again? Maybe. But he said it regardless of the motivation. He said it. And as the value of the NFL's franchises continue to go up and up and up, four years ago, Broncos sell for 4.65 billion. 3 years ago, Commanders sell for 6.05 billion. Now, Seahawks going for 9.612 something billion. As those values go up and up and up, there's more value in the minority shares that the Packers can't sell. And by comparison, the Packers are at a disadvantage. There is a solution. And I've been researching this. I've been talking to people about it. There is a solution. And I don't know that it'll ever happen. I don't know that it ever would happen. But could it happen? Yes. And it's very simple. You dissolve Green Bay Packers Incorporated and the Packers become an expansion team that someone pays $20 billion to take over and that person buys the assets of Green Bay Packers Inc. which go into the fund that is distributed to charity just like the proceeds of the sale of the Seahawks will be it's in the Articles of Incorporation, the Green Bay Packers Incorporated articles of incorporation which are easily found on Google. It's like a two-page document if that much. and it sets forth what happens in the event the corporation ever dissolves. You dissolve it and you replace it at the same time. It's already lined up in advance. Before you even dissolve the corporation, there's somebody who pays whatever the expansion fee would be. And the other owners would love that because they get money for nothing. They get 132nd of the expansion fee. and and incidental benefit. The Packers financial information must be publicly disclosed. With that, we extrapolate a lot of things about how the league is doing. The Packers are no longer a publicly owned company. That goes away and everything's secret after that. So, I think the league would like it. The reality is why would the people in charge of Green Bay Packers Incorporated ever do it? And here's the window for it to happen if it ever happens. They have a mandatory retirement age for the president and CEO. When Ed Policy approaches that number, I can't remember if it's 70, 67, whatever it is. When Ed policy approaches that number, he's leaving anyway. he's going to be out of a job anyway if he thinks that the long-term interests of the Green Bay Packers are served by a conversion of the business structure from corporation to this private entity. And look, you'd want to find a mega billionaire who loves the Green Bay Packers and wouldn't be inclined to move the team. That would be the risk that the Packers organization takes that at some point the owner of the Packers would leave Green Bay. But why? Why? Why would why? They still fill the stadium. They got a 50-year waiting list for tickets. They're a popular team nationally. Why would you do it? So the the last point I'll make on this, those shares of stock that are framed in various libraries and man caves and kitchens and wherever else people have their Green Bay Packer stock certificate. They would become meaningless. They would become worthless. But they already are. They already are. You still have the piece of paper. They're not going to go confiscate your stock certificate. It still would be a difficult thing to sell to the fan base. And part of the sale would be to get them to understand number one, nothing will change. And number two, having an owner who can sell off pieces of the team, who will have unlimited funds to pay for whatever is needed. Having that owner is better for the Packers. And this all comes back to where it started. If Ed policy is going to sound the alarm that the current financial realities of life in the NFL are making it harder for the Packers to compete, if you're a Packers fan, wouldn't you want the team to be owned by somebody who can compete? The president of the company is saying it. The guy in charge of the Packers is saying, "Hey, hey, hey, hey, we can't compete in this modern financial reality of the NFL." If I'm a Packers fan, I'm going to say, "What? What? How can we fix it? How can we fix it? This is a way to fix it." I'm not saying it should happen. I'm not saying it will happen. All I'm saying is it could happen. I've found nothing that would keep it from happening. The current management of Green Bay Packers Incorporated would have to be motivated to do it. And that leads to all sorts of speculation about backroom deals that may get enough of the members of the board of directors behind it. But regardless, it's not impossible. And if we do come to a time when the Packers just can't compete and it manifests itself in the kind of onfield struggles that we saw from the time Lombardi left until the time Brett Favre arrived. and they they turned it around with John Don Macowski, but it really took off with Favre, then Rogers, and now they're still they in the 70s they were an also ran. They they were a laughingstock. They they used to call remember Chris Burman called the Packers Buccaneers games the the Bay of Pigs. They both stunk in the early to mid 80s. And again, the Packers through most of the 70s weren't very good. If days like that would ever return and management is tying it back to this broader structure and overall financial wherewithal of the teams, it could happen. Packers fans, I'm thinking of you here. If your team does reach the point where it can't compete because of the current structure and the everinccreasing price and value of NFL franchises, there is a way out of it. And the easy way out, dissolve the corporation and find a multi-billionaire who is a card carrying cheese head who would buy that team and keep it in Green Bay for decades to come. Hi, it's Mike Florio. Thanks for watching PFT on YouTube. Hit subscribe for the latest news and analysis from Pro Football

title: Should NFL revamp Super Bowl postgame ceremony? | Pro Football Talk | NFL on NBC
text: A point I want to make about the postgame celebration, the ceremony, much more organized than what we see in the NFL.
